title: Doctor Knowall
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a poor peasant named Crabb, who drove a load of wood into town with two oxen and sold it to a doctor for two talers. As the money was being counted out to him, the doctor happened to be sitting at table, and when the peasant saw how well he ate and drank, his heart longed for what he saw, and he wished he could be a doctor too. So he stood there for a while, and finally asked whether he too could become a doctor. “Oh, yes,” said the doctor, “that’s easily done.” “What do I have to do?” asked the peasant. “First, buy yourself an A B C book, the kind with a rooster on the first page. Second, turn your cart and your two oxen into money, and get yourself some clothes and whatever else belongs to medicine. Third, have a sign painted that says ‘I am Doctor Knowall,’ and have it nailed up over your front door.” The peasant did everything he had been told. After he had practiced as a doctor for a short while, a rich and powerful lord had some money stolen. He was told about Doctor Knowall, who lived in such-and-such a village and must know what had become of the money. So the lord had the horses hitched to his carriage, drove out to the village, and asked Crabb whether he was Doctor Knowall. Yes, he said, he was. Then he was to come with the lord and get back the stolen money. “Oh, yes, but Grete, my wife, has to come too.” The lord agreed, gave both of them seats in the carriage, and they all drove off together. When they arrived at the nobleman’s castle, the table was set, and Crabb was told to sit down and eat. “Yes, but my wife, Grete, too,” he said, and he sat down at the table with her. When the first servant came in with a dish of fine food, the peasant nudged his wife and said, “Grete, that was the first,” meaning the servant who brought the first dish. The servant, however, thought he meant “That is the first thief,” and since he really was one, he was terrified. He said to his fellow servant outside, “The doctor knows everything. We’re in trouble. He said I was the first.” The second servant did not want to go in at all, but he was forced to. When he went in with his dish, the peasant nudged his wife and said, “Grete, that is the second.” This servant was just as alarmed and got out as fast as he could. The third did no better, for the peasant again said, “Grete, that is the third.” The fourth had to carry in a covered dish, and the lord told the doctor to show his skill and guess what was under the cover. There were crabs in it, in fact. The doctor looked at the dish, had no idea what to say, and cried, “Ah, poor Crabb.” When the lord heard that, he cried, “There! He knows it! Then he must also know who has the money!”

At this the servants looked terribly uneasy, and they signaled to the doctor that they wanted him to step outside for a moment. When he went out, all four of them confessed that they had stolen the money. They said they would gladly give it back and pay him a large sum besides, if he would not expose them, because if he did they would be hanged. They led him to the place where the money was hidden. The doctor was satisfied with this, went back into the hall, sat down at the table, and said, “My lord, now I will search in my book to find where the gold is hidden.” The fifth servant, however, had crept into the stove to find out whether the doctor knew even more. The doctor sat still and opened his A B C book, flipped the pages back and forth, and looked for the rooster. Since he couldn’t find it right away, he said, “I know you’re in there, so you had better come out!” The fellow in the stove thought the doctor meant him, and in a panic he jumped out, crying, “That man knows everything!” Then Doctor Knowall showed the lord where the money was, but did not say who had stolen it. He received a great deal of money as a reward from both sides, and became a famous man.
